utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Oric. Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with me, Jose Doria, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, and our case manager is assisted by Ms. Georgia Mirkovic, and she is for future our acting case manager and that is also the reason she is included now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, appearing for Mr. Naser Oric with Mr. John Jones. With us are our legal assistants, Ms. Jasmina Cosic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. This is the last week before we go on recess, so let's make the best use of the time available. How many witnesses do you have in town, or do you plan to have in town? How many witnesses do you have in town already, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We have, as far as I can oversee, there are three witnesses, and when it comes to those witnesses, the last in schedule is more or less standby at the end. I doubt whether we can finalise with the third one today, meaning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Okay. Okay. All right. Any preliminaries before we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You'll recall last week when Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Popovic testified that an issue arose as to a document bearing ERN numbers being provided to one of those witnesses, and we heard conflicting accounts of how the witness got the documents. Ratko Nikolic said that Nikola Popovic gave him the documents, quite emphatically he said that several times, whereas Mr. Popovic denied that. Now, the matter might just lie there and one would wonder which witness is mistaken and/or not telling the truth, but the fact is the Prosecution can actually throw some light on the matter, since firstly these documents bear ERN numbers and Mr. Di Fazio, in re-examining Mr. Nikolic, sought to suggest that in fact he provided the documents to Mr. Nikolic. And since, in our submission, it's important -- it's an important matter because it's important to know whose credibility is affected. Is it Mr. Popovic's or Mr. Nikolic's? We would submit that Mr. Di Fazio could clarify this matter as to whether in fact he did provide the documents to Mr. Nikolic, and if so, which documents, which is a very important matter, since you may recall Mr. Nikolic on occasion said, I didn't know who this man was until I saw the documents, or I wasn't sure of the date until I saw the documents. So which documents he provided, and also why he provided the documents. Because, as I understand it, or I assume that's not customary practice to provide documents to witnesses, but I don't know. But in any event, it seems that we shouldn't be left up in the air as to whether Mr. Popovic was mistaken or whether Mr. Nikolic was mistaken. We should have some clarification from the Prosecution as to what in fact happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not asking the Prosecution to deal with now on the hoof, because after all it's also Mr. Di Fazio who said that he personally provided the documents, but I think a considered response would be helpful in the coming days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that Mr. Wubben will refer this to Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. And we'll get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, of course, stands neutral on this matter. We will not give any direction, directives or any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. I simply raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And obviously, we'll play it by the ear as we go along and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was just that it seemed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I think it's very fit and proper for you to have raised the matter because it's there. Yes. Any further preliminary matters you would like to raise? Nothing. I see none. Usher, could you escort the witness in, please. Mr. Wubben, how much more do you think you need this witness for?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, three-quarters of an hour, one hour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In fact it will be me, and I imagine an hour, maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if we try to, without imposing on you, obviously, because we have already consumed 10, 12 minutes, leave it. We'll take as much time as we need. We'll take as much time as we need. What I was going to suggest is to try and finish with him by the break. But that's maybe asking too much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Let him sit down, usher. Let him sit down straight away. Make sure that he is on channel 4 -- channel -- whichever channel is his language. Good morning to you, Mr. Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] God bless you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you too. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] God bless you all again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you confirm to me that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what you're telling me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in your language of what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. But if she doesn't understand anything that I'm saying because the Serbo-Croat is the most difficult language in the world, the same thing has five or six different names. So people may not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that you are understanding what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, look at me, please. Mr. Wubben will be continuing and finishing his examination-in-chief, and when he's finished, then Mr. Jones, who is appearing for Naser Oric, will cross-examine you. May I just remind you of two things that I told you last time. One thing is that you are testifying under the solemn declaration that you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond made, that you entered last Friday, namely, that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. A solemn declaration that, in some jurisdictions, is called an oath. The second thing I want to tell you and remind you of is that unless you want to stay here another two or three days, please restrict your answers to the question that is put to you. Just answer the question, and nothing else but the question. Otherwise we will be here for eternity. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand you, but I have not come here to get someone to light my cigarette. I came here to describe everything that happened in the area, if you see my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point, but it is not like that here. Here you are asked questions and you answer the questions. Otherwise, unfortunately, if I see that you are not prepared to abide by the rules, I will just send you home packing. Mr. Wubben, you may proceed with your first question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one matter which is -- again, this witness, despite being apparently illiterate, seems to have papers and documents in front of him which he seems to be looking at and perhaps preparing to refer to. I don't think it would be proper during the course of his testimony for him to be referring to papers and documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what he's going to -- why anticipate matters. When we come to that, Mr. Jones, we'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But Your Honour, he may be refreshing his memory as we speak from documents. It seems he should put those away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you see him refreshing his memory, just draw my attention, that's all, and we'll deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm seeing it now. He was just looking at the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What papers were you looking at, Mr. Miladinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ones that I have in front of me. These are papers, papers of houses that burnt down in the village of Jezestica. I wrote down each individual name on Friday of the owners when I left the courtroom. I kept writing until 1.00 in the morning. Because I don't like those photographs. They don't seem too accurate to me. Next thing, I have names, how things were taken away from people and a child too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see those papers. Let's -- usher, please bring them over and then we'll give them back to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you can read these. It's a pointless exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just -- let me decide, Mr. Miladinovic. I am the Judge, not you. Yes. Usher, please show them to Mr. Wubben and show them to Mr. Jones very quickly. And then return them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please give those papers back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think anyone could quite find their way around these papers that I wrote. Did you find what I wrote about this child being taken away? It's there, but I don't think you'd find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you write those yourself, Mr. Miladinovic, or did someone else write them for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote them personally, in my room, after dinner, and I kept on writing until 1.00 in the morning. I wanted to draw a map for you too, but I would have needed a much larger piece of paper in order to draw the entire village. If I'd known that we would need that, I would have found a man in Bratunac who would have done it for me. What you have here is something that I drew personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I thought last Friday you told us that you are illiterate, you can't read or write, and you can only distinguish some block letters -- let me finish, please. You said that you can only distinguish some block letters, capital letters. And then I see that practically almost everything is written cursive, small letters, continuous writing. Anyway, Mr. Wubben, he is your witness, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Wubben: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, will you please tell me when you gave a statement on Friday, last Friday, regarding the attack of the 8th of August, 1992, you gave information to the Judges about the attack. My next question will be the time after that attack, and my question will be: In the period after, following up after the 8th of August, 1992, did any JNA or VRS army or force come to the village to speak to the villagers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the village guards still remain keeping guard after the 8th of August, 1992, so after that attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With me, there were eight persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did those nine persons in total, or eight persons, keep --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight. I said eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This group of village guards, did they remain keeping guard every day or keeping up the system like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until Christmas-time, until Christmas-time. Everything remained the same. They slept at Nikola's house. I said that on the 8th there were two or three houses left. My own, Nikola's and Nikola uncle's, the guard slept there over there in his house and I slept in my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the village guard receive any new weaponry or military equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No equipment. Some rubber boots, that sort of thing, and shirts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated the time period until Christmas. What happened in Christmas, following up --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then? Was there an attack or not? Please confirm.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're asking me. Can you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at Christmas following up this attack of August? Was there a new attack or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. When you say -- because let's be specific, Mr. Wubben. Be patient a little bit with the Trial Chamber and with the witness. When you say Christmas, precisely exactly which day of the year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The date, please. Because Christmas for me that year was the 25th of December. I'm sure that for the witness it wasn't the 25th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I mean the beginning of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but could you just mention the day and the month, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I didn't took the liberty to lead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Lead him. Lead him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an attack on the 7th of January, on Christmas in 1993, on your village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to describe that, don't you, how it was, or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Go ahead. Yes, please. But first of all tell us whether there was an attack on the 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly on the 7th of January. It's the Serbian Christmas, the Catholic Christmas falls on the 25th. There was an attack at half past Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond 5.00. I was standing guard at the time. We were surrounded on all sides, and there was just one side towards Polom that you could escape to. At half past 5.00, there were white and black uniforms like the ones we had. I was not able to see the fires. You can see the hill of Tanici, you can see the whole of Kravica from there, but not Jaglici because there's a hill in between. You can see the river Drina and Cizmici and Jesova and Glogova. You can see everything. That's the sort of view we have from there. So that's how it began. The shooting began. You had nowhere to go. It was Christmas-time, so we were roasting pigs. We needed some meat to eat. Those Turks didn't even allow us to have breakfast. That's how early they started attacking us. So then we had to run to the bottom of the village. 17 persons were killed there. If you want any detail on this, I can provide some. 17. One was taken away to Srebrenica, to see Naser, but he never came back alive. That's why I had gone to Mitar Nikolic's house. I was sitting there and watched the cowsheds and then barns and house burning. I watched it all. There were about 20 women crying out and yelling: We'll never be able to build these houses again. I came by and I said: Well, sure we'll put these houses up again at some point. The main thing is to remain alive. And they left towards Polom. Mitar and myself remained. There was a cowshed there. I had oxen that I kept. I wanted nothing but a box of cigarettes, and I had wheat too, but I needed no more wheat, because I had enough. I would give it away to people, and my oxen would be used to draw firewood and they said: Do you want some firewood? And I said: No, all I want is a box of cigarettes. And then I saw my cowshed burning and I thought to myself: My oxen must be burning. But actually, someone had taken the livestock away as I was later to find out. And I said: Come on, the two of us must go too. And he said: I don't want to leave the house. I'd rather just burn it down. And I said: No. Don't burn your house. Let them burn it if they want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a question for you related to those white uniform -- sorry - I'll redress that question. I have a question to you, Witness, related to those men attacking the village. They were dressed in white and black uniforms. And you referred to them as Turks. Were these Muslim forces or other forces? Can you tell us more about the ethnicity of these forces attacking your village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In World War II, we called them Turks. Tito, if you've heard of that ruler of Yugoslavia, allowed them to be undeclared. Later, he allowed them to be Muslims. Their wives covered themselves, but he ordered them and they had to uncover themselves. But I don't know what faith they are. How should I call them? They call themselves Bosniaks now. But I'm also from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Muslim or Turks attackers did you notice? Was this a huge number or small groups or one group? Please tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a small group. There were thousands, thousands. Because from my hill, I could see everything around me was burning. I could see the entire Kravica area and the Tanici. And if you don't believe me, you could send someone and see how visible it was from that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to the area of the Jezestica village, how much is the number then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number of attackers? Because you described the number of attackers to your estimation when it comes to the entire Kravica area, but we are now here dealing with the Jezestica area or village.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not less than a thousand there either, because this is a large area. The village of Jezestica has 504 citizens, 120 houses, some people have two, some have six. I used to have six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was all burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question will indeed be related to that burning. Did you actually saw the houses being burnt and also the reason how they had been torched or not, or was there another cause of that fire of the houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut it down into different questions. Mr. Miladinovic, look at me, please. Did you see houses -- did you just see houses burning or did you also see houses being set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw them burning houses. They carried some kind of liquid and then the house would start burning right away. I saw about six people in olive-grey uniforms. They had some kind of short-barrelled weapons. I served in the army. I only knew about the 48. I didn't know about this other weapon. It's a short-barrelled kind of weapon with a magazine at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The previous answer of the witness was and it was all surrounded, not it was all burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you actually saw people setting these houses on fire, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Does that answer your question, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About this group of persons in olive-grey uniforms, did they cooperate together with the others dressed in black and white uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are confusing the terms. This was for Christmas, at Christmas, but it's something else on the 8th of August. I think it's a little confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Be patient with us, Mr. Miladinovic. We are still referring to what happened on Christmas Day, the Serb Orthodox Christmas Day, 7th of January. On the 7th of January, I just want you to confirm the following: You saw large number of attackers, you said round about 1.000 attacking the village of Jezestica and its surroundings. Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you also said that these persons, these attackers, were wearing white and black uniforms like you were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also said that on that occasion, on the 7th of January, 1993, you saw a large number of houses burning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Amongst those houses and the property burning, you also saw your own, including the farm where you had the ox?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see those houses. They're a little bit covered. I have three houses there, but there is a hill in front of them. So I couldn't see that. But I saw the other two in Versica [phoen]. I have to be precise. I would like to be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I really appreciate that an elderly man of your age has got still such a good and vivid memory and wishes to be so precise in his answers. I wish many other witnesses were like you, Mr. Miladinovic. You also told us that you saw a number of persons, round about six persons, setting some of the houses on fire with some kind of cans or things that they were carrying with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you said that the persons that were setting these houses on fire were wearing olive-drab uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, coming back to what Mr. Wubben wanted to ask you: Were these six persons who were torching these houses separate from the group of attackers or did they form part of the group of attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were close together, all of them. It's just that these were going around and burning, and the people who were going in front were killing people. The others were throwing people out of their houses. And there was another group, a third group, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that was taking things out of the houses and burning. They were a very well organised group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The group that were taking things out of the houses, what were they -- first of all, were they just men or were there also women amongst them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The women were carrying things; women, children, they were banging buckets and they were shouting like they were in some sort of chase, like they were chasing a bear or something. They were saying: Get the Chetniks. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Were there any men amongst them, the ones who were taking things out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there were men there. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what were those men wearing, the ones who were taking -- the ones who were taking things out of the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were all kinds of things. They were also wearing civilian uniforms. I said so. Women were carrying things and throwing things out. People were taking away flour, everything that they needed, things for eating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the third group, those who you said were attacking and killing people, what were those wearing? What were those wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you're asking me the other way round. The first group was going around and beating people up. The second group was entering the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first group. Let's take them one by one, Mr. Miladinovic. The first group, according to you, the ones who were beating people, beating people up and killing, what -- were they just men or were they men and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Men. The women were in the rear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And these men who were beating people up and who were in the front, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Black, white. They had all sorts of clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Was there snow on the ground on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 50 centimetres, if you know what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So that was the first group. The second group was the group that were entering houses, you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And what were they entering houses for? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. They were taking things out that they needed. They wouldn't burn bread, if you know what wheat bread or cornbread is, beans. They would take better care of the bread than the Serbs did. Because they appreciated the bread. They will burn everything once they take the bread out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And these people who were entering the houses and taking the bread out, were they just men or were they mixed? Were there women amongst them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only men. The elderly men were taking -- carrying things out and the women were taking them away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And these men that were entering houses, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were they wearing civilian clothes or uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some had uniforms, the odd rifle. They had to have one. And there were all sorts of different clothing that they wore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have spoken of two groups. How many other groups were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, at this stage we don't know where the witness was when he saw all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will be asking him. Don't worry. This is to try and clear up and try -- it might seem that it's going to take longer, but in actual fact it's going to take shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It might be one house we're talking about and one group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd hate the impression to be created that this witness is describing a whole panorama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that, Mr. Jones. Don't worry. But this witness also told us with regard to his houses, his six houses, that some he couldn't see, so he wouldn't testify upon, and others he did. So that was the prelude, actually, why I have taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could be accurate here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we've spoken of two groups, the ones who were beating people up and then the second group who was entering houses. Now, how many other groups were there, if there were any other groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said three groups. The third group was carrying things away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that you described already, where they were mainly women and children, but also some men together with them, mostly wearing civilian clothes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, from these three groups, which of the groups was torching the houses, or were those six persons you referred to before a separate group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the second group. I think you didn't understand me. They were throwing things out of the houses and burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- no, no. I had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once they took what they were supposed to take away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had understood you perfectly, but it's you who is giving evidence and not I, so it's you who has to make the statements, Mr. Miladinovic, and not me. Next question: You saw these persons entering houses, taking the bread out, and then setting them on fire and taking things out and setting them on fire. How many houses did you see these persons setting on fire, roughly? I don't want you to be precise to the nearest decimal point, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have 84 in my papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that basically means that you saw these six persons, roughly, going inside 84 houses and setting those 84 houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 84. Perhaps I didn't see -- I didn't have that visibility. I personally saw 10 to 15 houses, but 84 altogether were burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. Now, would you be in a position to give us the names of the owners of the houses, those 10 to 15 houses that you saw being set on fire, only those 10 to 15 for the time being, please? Mr. Wubben, I'm sure you don't mind me taking him over for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's why I sat down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand this last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sorry if I did not make myself very clear to you, Mr. Miladinovic. I apologise to you. You said that you saw about 10 to 15 houses with your own eyes being torched, being set on fire by those six persons in olive-drab uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand me correctly again. I said that I didn't have the visibility. I didn't see all the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond houses being burned, those 10 to 15 houses, but I did say that you could see there was a lot of flames everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which houses did you actually see being set on fire, being torched, with your own eyes? Can you be specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to tell you from the top of my head? I don't need to look at the papers. Would you like me to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on Christmas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Only those houses, Mr. Miladinovic, that you saw with your own eyes being set on fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I read them out one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This witness said that he wrote down those lists on Friday night. I don't see any reason why on Friday night he should have been able to recall from memory which houses he saw set on fire and now should be unable to need to refer to a piece of paper. If he genuinely saw -- which it seems blindingly obvious to us he didn't see any houses being burnt personally, but if he did, surely he can tell us now which houses those were, if he wrote it down on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How old is your grandfather, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My grandparents are deceased, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, do you really need to look at those papers? Can you remember the names without having to look at those papers? After all, you said there were very few houses that you saw being set on fire with your own eyes. Do you remember those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that on the 8th of August, when I was, that's how it was. But now this is Christmas. We're talking about Christmas now. You're taking me back and forth all the time. I didn't come to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are still on the 7th of January of 1993. I am not taking you back to August. Please stay on the 7th of January, 1993. On that occasion, which houses did you see with your own eyes being set on fire, on Christmas Day, Orthodox Christmas Day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miladinovic, Dragomir, two houses. Miladinovic Nikola, one house. Milanovic Rajo, one house. Bozidar Vukcic [phoen] one house. Dragan Milanovic, one house. Milisav Djukanovic, one house. Nedjo Milanovic, one house. Vojislav Milanovic, one house. Cedo Milanovic, one house. Pero Ostojic. Trisic Slavorad. Bozidar Djuric. Vasilije Djokic, Mila Djokic, Sreten Djokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's enough. Earlier on in your testimony, you also said that during the attack on Christmas Day, on the 7th of January, 17 of your fellow citizens and villagers were killed during the attack. Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you just, without looking at papers, tell us the names, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What papers? It's not here in the papers. It's here in my head. Shall I tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight brothers were killed there. Vaso Miladinovic, two Ostojics, two Djukanovics, two Bogicevics, and I was the one who was placing them in the bags. I'm not going to repeat that. It's already written. Vida Trisic. Then Nevenka Djukanovic, Ivan Djukanovic, Bosko Djukanovic, Kico Djukanovic. No, no. I'm not finished yet. Milo Jokic, Mitar Nikolic. I don't know if that's 17. Could you please check, because I will remember. I know all the names. Of course I know the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's more than enough, Mr. Miladinovic. And now I am going to hand you back to Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And incidentally, when these persons were killed, in other words, during the peak of the attack, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was at Mitar Nikolic's place, and I've already said that before. But I will say it again. When all of that was burning, we left his house. I almost got killed. I was the one. But he didn't. He had the protection so that he was protected from bullets. I went the other way. But bullets were whizzing past, but none of them hit me. But it -- I couldn't have cared less if they hit me or not. But then I crossed over a small creek and then I saw that they will not kill me. At about noon, I arrived at Zagoni. It started when Nikola Miladinovic and Lazo Milanovic were there. We spent the night. I didn't even know the first or last name of that man. And then in the morning I left for Bratunac. We were walking. We were going on foot. There was half a metre of snow. We arrived at Bratunac. And those people whom I mentioned who had been killed were not coming. My two sons were not coming either. I was wandering around once I got to Bratunac. There was some food to eat in Bratunac, and I was there. And on the 10th, they took me away to work in the Red Cross, to find accommodation, shelter, for women, children, to give them food, to provide them with mattresses, blankets. And I was there. After 70 days, I went to see what had happened over there and where they were killed. I found that. The lawyer has all the names and last names, and I was putting the papers in those black bags. And then it went to the administration. I went to Bratunac. General Morillon also came to the funeral. This was really terrible. But the lawyers have it all, how their heads were cut off and ribs, my son's head was cut off, both of his arms were cut off. His ribs, he was missing one leg. And then I found it the next day. This is very sad, but what can I say? They shouldn't have done that. If you killed him, all right, kill him and then just move on, but this is really sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This Mitar Nikolic's house, where was it in relation to the centre of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's at the bottom of the village and he could escape to Siljkovici. There's a boundary there, if you know what I'm saying, between the two fields. He's at the bottom of the village, Mitar Nikolic, if you understand my point. That's where the village of Jezestica begins, from Kravica on, and then on to Siljkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in relation to your house and the farm where you had the ox, Mitar Nikolic's house, I want to know. Where was it in relation to your house and the farm where you had the ox? How far was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where Mitar was, further up there were oxen there belonging to a man named Bogicevic and another one name Pajic, and his mother. They were farming the land and he took the livestock away, tied them up and gave them food. And he said we could take anything they like. All I wanted was a box of cigarettes. I needed no money at that point. A man offered me 3.000 German marks but I said: I have no use for this money. I never thought it would come to that. I had no idea that this would ever come to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Miladinovic. Mr. Wubben will take over again now, please. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you described that property has been taken away during that attack. What happened to the cattle and can you tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, when I thought that my oxen had been set on fire, that wasn't actually what happened. They were taking livestock away for their own benefit. But did I tell you that at Pale my cow was found? And the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond oxen. They never burned down. A man took them away and then set fire to the cowshed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And witness --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have very accurate information of what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have a question regarding the other houses, farmhouses with cattle. Did you notice that also other cattle had been taken away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything. All the livestock was taken away. Nothing remained. And they wouldn't kill them either. Like I said a while ago, on the 20th of June, the three houses were set fire to. One of them belonged to me and two to my neighbours. They took all the livestock away and they shot the pigs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Witness, we are now dealing with this Christmas attack, so you can confirm that attackers took cattle away, can you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- a question related to the damage to your village, the village of Jezestica, including the hamlet. To what extent did the attack cause damage to the village? Was the whole village burned down or partly of it? Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Perhaps about 20 houses, 80 per cent damage, some had 100 per cent damage, some had 20 per cent damage, but most of the houses had 100 per cent damage, which means razed to the ground. Because they were made of wood. If you see my point. And those that were built of hard material, 80 per cent, 20 per cent, 50 per cent, depending. Let me be specific about that. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court that around half of the houses had been burned down by the attack in August. Does that mean that the remaining part of the village has been burned down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August, 50 houses were burned, 50. 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The remaining houses had been burned down during the Christmas attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they burned everything, everything, one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, and what happened, Witness, with the barns and stables? Also being burned down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was left standing. Not a single chicken, if you know what I mean. You can come over and see for yourselves. There is nothing left there, if you get my meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would like to show some photographs to the witness. May I please request the usher's assistance to tender a number of six photographs out of the range of exhibit number P3 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want any photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: P365, and that's in reuse again. Your Honour, it will be on Sanction as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we will be following in Sanction, and the witness, however, would like to be shown the originals that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What use do I have for these photographs? Why would I need these?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, because we require you to see these -- to have a look at these photos.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have perhaps the centre of Jezestica so you can show me how they smashed the memorial plaques.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will show you the photos that we have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will show you the photos that we have one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Drago Djuric, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, the first photograph will be ERN number 010 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just mention the last four digits, Mr. Wubben. 7842.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 7842, confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, I want to make sure that the witness has in front of him the photo ending with the four digits 7842. He does. Mr. Miladinovic, do you recognise that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Vidosav's house and this is Drago's house. This is the same. Can't you see? What are you giving me these for? This is Vidosav's house and the other one is Drago's house. There's nothing for me to tell there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do you complicate matters unnecessarily? Can't you give the witness the photos one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, shall I give the usher my serial so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do I need to be talking about these?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, please do it for my sake. You know how difficult my job --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I really appreciate -- I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, we are looking at this house, the one which has the ERN number 7842. Can you please tell me whose house that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one, you mean? This one? Drago Djuric's house, from Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what he saw; no? Okay. Thank you. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Next one will be 7843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court whose house this is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vidosav Bogicevic's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, these two houses -- one moment. These two houses, when were they rendered into this condition? When did they finish up like that? In August? In January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 7th of January. The damage occurred on the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can he be specific as to the damage. I mean that last house is virtually -- perhaps the witness could be specific as to what damage he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He doesn't need to. I mean, I don't imagine that he went in to inspect the damage. Then it's a question of whether there is enough evidence whether this house has been damaged or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's a certain danger in the broad brush approach that he'll say everything was destroyed on those two dates, and we have no photographic evidence whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, this last house that you've just seen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you about this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. When do you think this photo was taken? Have you got an idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No idea. I don't have any information on that. I was the first to return to Jezestica, and then people from 20 other households returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I was among the first in 1996 to return to my land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think that this photo shows the condition in which the house was after the attack of 7th January? Is this house -- is this how this house ended up after the attack, or did it look different Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond than what we see on the photo here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It looked better when it was first built. Can't you see it's burned and charred? It doesn't look much. All the woodwork was taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to the next document, Mr. Wubben, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 7845, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now again, Mr. Miladinovic, do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- what do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Whether you recognise that building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Milan Djukanovic's house. No one even gave him any money. This is how the house is now, and he has to live in it like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when was this house destroyed like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 7th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993. 1993. I'm sorry. Early 1993, the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Miladinovic. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Next one is 7851.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, whose house is that, Mr. Miladinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the one in the front.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mile Rankovic's house. Mile Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when was it destroyed like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The windows and the doors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. When --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Was it destroyed like that or damaged like that on the 7th of January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Behind it there seems to be another building. I don't know if it's a house or whether it's a shed or whatever. Do you recognise that other building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do. There's an oven. It's something like a summer kitchen. There's an oven there for when it's hot in the house. There's a small table outside. Do you know how many times I sat there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And whose -- does it belong to the same house or is it a separate property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please clarify? I'm not sure what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This building -- in this photo, we see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm clear about the house, and you see his land here too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the building behind the house, did it belong -- did it belong to the same house, to the same owner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was it damaged --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same owner. Same owner as the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it damaged --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an oven, a stove. In this outbuilding, we'd brew coffee there. We'd sit outside in the summer to have coffee at this table in summertime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it damaged too during the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that it was damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next photo, 7874. Whose house is that, Mr. Miladinovic? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd need to have a closer look first. You can't have a blind man tell you things straight away before he's even had a look. This is Ljubisav Djuric's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was it damaged on the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's from Gajici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it damaged on the same occasion, on Christmas Day of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Christmas Day. Everything was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next photo, 7878.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recognise this one. Maybe Vaso Bogicevic's house, but I can't be sure about it. I can't be sure about it. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was Vaso Bogicevic's house, and it may still be. It's just that I can't be certain about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry, about Mr. Miladinovic. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I come to the finalising part of my exam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: See if you can conclude by half 10.00, please. If you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It will certainly be possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you stated for the Court that 17 persons had been killed and you gave details about their names. Did you saw the dead bodies actually upon your return to Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- whether or not --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I can tell you everything. I picked up every single body and put it in a bag. But please, you never mentioned that one man was sent over to report to Naser Oric, but never came back. I think this matter needs clarifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I give you permission to tell us the story, but in not more than one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, please. Let me -- I'm -- I've taken him over for most of the time for every specific reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. It's just that in all of the statements we've been disclosed by this witness he's never dealt with this incident at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are entitled to ask him why he never mentioned it before. If you are interested in the matter. Because at the end of the day, you may not be. Mr. Miladinovic, this man or this person, because I don't know who this person was who was supposed to go and report to Naser, as you said, and never came back, tell us the story, but in one minute, please, because we have got other persons waiting to come and give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragoje Lazic from the village of Jezestica. That's all I have to say about that. Drago Lazic. I can tell you straight off. He never came back. Is that fast enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want me to tell you about the other people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No more now. Last few questions from Mr. Wubben and then you can have a break and we can have a break too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those persons that you saw, those persons that had been killed [Microphone not activated], were they dressed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will repeat. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those persons that you saw that had been killed, those 17 persons that you mentioned, how were they dressed? Were they dressed in uniforms or not, civilian clothes or partly, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending. Some people had civilian clothes and some people had uniforms. What do I know? But I can tell you their names. I picked them up one by one. I'll be quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have already told us their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell you about me picking them up and putting their bodies in bags. 70 days later I came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You told us as well, Mr. Miladinovic. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Those uniforms that you noticed, were these uniforms of a specific army or uniforms that village guards might use or someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was olive-drab, the old kind, Tito's uniform. That should have been thrown away long ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever been compensated for the damage that you suffered from this attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No compensation has arrived, just like World War II. My father was killed in Jasenovac, my mother and my three sisters were killed in the village. 121 casualties in the village of Jezestica. No one paid any sort of compensation. That was World War II and now our grandchildren repeated the very same thing, 45 of my relatives died in the village. But as for the bodies that I picked up, I have a whole list. I went and picked up one by one, name by name. Please, if you can grant me that small request. I'll be done in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a specific question related to that compensation. Do you know of anyone else from your village that got compensation or a promise for compensation of the damage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be accurate about this. Two of my sons were killed. Some people claimed damages and received damages. I never did, nor do I need any of that. I can't bring my children back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tell the Court that some of them got damages, do you mean that they got compensation from the government for that damage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, as for money to rebuild their houses, no. No. No one is giving that kind of money away, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was my last question, but I notice that there was an urgent need by this witness for limited time to express some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Miladinovic, you were anxious to tell us the names of the persons that you collected and put in bags to be buried, to be given a decent burial. Yes, I will allow you to give us the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you so much. Krsto Djukanovic. I found him outside the house, mutilated. I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness is simply going to give a list of names, that's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me finish, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Provided it's clear that our client isn't charged with any crimes against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. You don't need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the public that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But you mentioned reconciliation last time and this is part of it as well. Yes, Mr. Miladinovic, please. Mr. Miladinovic, look at me, please, and proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I found Bosko Djukanovic; the same thing, just the bones. Everything else had been cut away. Then I found Vida Trisic, a lady. There were just some clothes and bones, so I threw them into a bag. I found Nevenka Djukanovic, some clothes and bones. Same thing. And then there were some sort of a dam there and next to the dam I found Ivan Djukanovic. His lower jawbone, that was all, and his watch and I put it all into a bag. That was after the 8th. I recognised his watch. He had two little sons. And I said: We'll give this to his children, let them have it. And then Neod Danila's [phoen] house. There was a ditch there in which I found Vojo Bogicevic. There was almost nothing there. And next to him I found Nedjo Milanovic. His body was not that damaged really. I put them all in a bag. And then I found Radomir. Just next to the ditch, Radomir Jovanovic. He was also not in a good state. And then I found one of the sons. His arm had been severed. Both his arms had been severed. So was his head. His ribs. Only the upper portion of the spine, and I found one of the -- one of his legs the next day and put it in a bag. I found Gordan Nikolic whole. And then I headed further down and there was something there. I'm not sure how to put it. People were building the wall of a house there and there were cables sticking out. And whoever it was ran off, because they were afraid that the wall was mined. I didn't want to run. I found one of the sons, but not the other. And then I took a stick and with my hands I dug the earth up until I found the body. I found Radojko Bogicevic. His throat had been cut, but his body had not been mutilated. And then I found my other son. He worked in Bratunac, at the sawmill. Maybe they had worked together. He pulled him on the ground by a scarf. And then there was another one, Dragan Milanovic, a small boy, 16 years of age. I found him there. He was trying to run. And in Opravdici, the village of Opravdici, they caught up with Mile Jokic. I picked his body up too. Mitar Ostojic, I picked his body up too. And Mitar Ostojic, yes. That's where I picked them up. And I saw also Miladin Momcilovic. His head had been cut off, lying next to him. I'm not sure if you get my meaning. A dog guarded his body for 70 days. That's what I did. These are all the names. And the man who had to go to Srebrenica never returned, the one I spoke about earlier. Please, the whole thing was taken away to Kravica, the bodies. And there was a doctor down there who examined the bodies, and everything was taken to Bratunac. There was General Morillon, who was present when the coffins were being put into the ground. Father and son. There was a lot of mourning and crying. Here you have my explanation. Thank you very much for giving me this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Miladinovic. We will now have a 30-minute -- 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. 30-minute break because we have a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Miladinovic, Mr. Jones now is going to put to you a number of questions. Yes, Mr. Wubben. I'm sorry. I didn't recognise you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's okay, Your Honour. Registry requested me, if it's possible, to tender the six photographs to the Court, the six photographs being used by showing the photographs, and you will -- you have noticed that in the beginning there was some confusion, so the best way to proceed is to tender these into evidence and to give it a special number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have a special number for these photos, Mr. Gerold Siller.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben; I thank you, Mr. Siller. So be it. Those six documents will have that exhibit number, 461 [realtime transcript read in error "641"]. Or 461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying it because the transcript says 641. That's wrong. It's 461. Yes, Mr. Jones. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, I'm going to be asking you some questions. I'd be grateful if you'd keep your answers as short as possible. In many instances, you can give a simple yes/no answer. If that's clear.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something. I didn't finish, and then you gave somebody else to question me. I forgot one person that I put in the bag, Milovan Ostojic. Please don't consider me to be something else. I still have relatives who were killed in Zagoni. I told the lawyer that. I'm asking you kindly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough now. Mr. Jones, please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miladinovic, you referred yesterday when you were speaking of the attack on your village on the 8th of August, 1992, to seeing a person on a white horse, and you said that it might be Golic from Glogova. So I'm going to start by asking you some questions about Golic from Glogova. Now, were you referring to Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ejub Golic was an important figure in Glogova, wasn't he; that's why you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Cizmici, so-called Bijeceva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, wasn't he the commander of the Muslims from Glogova in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, whether he was a commander or not. I only heard that recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right, though, that on the 8th of August, 1992, you thought that the attack might be from the Muslims from Glogova, might have been coming from the Muslims from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not so. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, why --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't understand me. I can tell you where he's from, if you would like to know. From Cizmici, Pale, Jaglici, Susnjari. That's where the attack came from. Why are you taking me back to Glogova? I didn't come here to lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right that on the day, you thought the attack was coming from the Muslims from Cizmici and Jaglici, that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, from local Muslims, from near your village, your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were stories, weren't there, of Golic having a white horse and being a local commander, and that's why you thought that it might be him on the white horse?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Naser had a white horse, and he was in Brezak Brijeg on the 8th of August and maybe he gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what you told us yesterday, Mr. Miladinovic. You told us that you saw a white horse and you said --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said: Whether it was Golic from Glogova or another man, I don't know. But you also said that he was far away, as far as a kilometre away, and that you couldn't actually see who it was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either Naser or this Ejub Golic, whatever his name is. You're just confusing me. Because he did have a white horse. So you can ask General Morillon. He knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't wish to confuse you, but I will ask you a question about your eyesight, since we're talking about distances. You told the Court on Friday that you had an operation on your eyes three years ago, so you had a problem with your eyesight before then which required surgery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm going to get the document out. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait, wait. I have the piece of paper. I wouldn't know how to measure into grammes. I was working in the Red Cross. I have a document here. For five years, from 1993, the 10th of January, I joined the Red Cross. I wouldn't be able to measure. I mean, I didn't have glasses then. Only when I went home did this problem begin. And I have a document. If you're interested, you can call the Red Cross in Bratunac. The president is there. It's very easy to prove. If you're trying to convince me that I'm blind, that I couldn't see, then we could disprove that. Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not trying to persuade you that you're blind. It's right, isn't it, that you didn't have perfect vision in August 1992, 20/20 vision, did you? You're not telling us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you're taking me back. I have just told you: How could I possibly see to weigh down to a gramme if I had problems with my vision? It's a shame what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. Isn't another reason why you thought that the attacking forces might be led by Golic, Ejub Golic, was because the Serbs in your area had been fighting with the Muslims from Glogova and some other places from the outbreak of war right up to August 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that always I call them Turks. The Muslims were undeclared. The Bosniaks. I know in World War II, as children we called them Turks. Later, Tito permitted them to be undeclared. Then he allowed them to be Muslims. Now they're Bosniaks. I'm a Bosnian too. I don't know how to refer to them. Did you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did. But if you would please try and keep your answers short. That's not the question I asked you. I was asking about the Muslims in Glogova, and in that regard, I'm going to put a question to you, and I remind you that you are under oath and I'd appreciate an honest answer. You do know, don't you, that the Muslims from Glogova were expelled from their homes in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May. Which May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May 1992. You've told us you could see Glogova from your village. You're aware, aren't you, that all the Muslims from Glogova were expelled in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw that happening, the Muslims being expelled, their houses being burnt, people being killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see it. I was down in the village. I didn't come out to see that. I was down in the village. I didn't come out to watch. I just said that on the 5th, I went to Bukova Glava for a saint's feast day. I went there. And 25 households were expelled from their and burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, Mr. Miladinovic. My question is very simple: Are you aware that the Muslims in Glogova were expelled from their homes in May 1992? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't know about that, because I wasn't there. I was in Tanici. And I had three houses there in the field, so I didn't really move away from there for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A simple "yes," "no," or "I don't know" will suffice. We'll come back to that. Now, on the 8th of August, 1992, when the attack started, you were in Mile Djukanovic's house in Brdo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. No. I was in my house and I saw them burning those houses. Again, you're taking me back, but you should ask me about the truth. How could I have been at Mile Tanic's? His house was being set on fire and I was supposed to be in his house. But I have my own house, which is 20 to 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to establish, Mr. Miladinovic, where you were when the attack started. So you say you were in your house in Tanici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just remind him, make it clear to him that we are dealing now only for the purpose of this question with the 8th of August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
