utterances.text: Now, what you call Brdo, in Jezestica, the hill, that was on the front lines, wasn't it, facing the Muslim villages of Jaglici and Cizmici?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think -- I hate to interrupt, but I don't think the witness will understand what's included in this question, that is also a kind of awareness of being confronted with front lines. I don't know what my learned friend means by that. It is the first time it comes up and it is now slotted in in this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see, because you are drawing conclusions for the witness who is by no means someone to be underestimated. So put the question again, please. The witness is fully aware of what he is being asked. If he has a problem, he will tell me and I will clear things up for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, you've spoken of the villages of Jaglici and Cizmici, which are Muslim villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were right across from your village, Jezestica, which is a Serb village; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm getting at is this: Isn't it --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please explain it to me differently. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that in August 1992 there were lines, trenches, in your village in order to defend against an attack, let's say, from Cizmici or Jaglici? That was your line, defence line.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know. I said -- I told these lawyers I was looking after the oxen, harvesting the corn, feeding the cattle, by myself. I was there just to prevent anybody from coming in and strangling the women. On the 8th of August, the wife had fallen asleep. I woke her up. But it would have all burned in a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, do you know what trenches are? Trenches.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trenches. Yes, I know what they are. I saw them being dug by people in Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Trenches were also in Jezestica, weren't they? You had trenches.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were there later, but not at that time. There's only a road which goes quite deep and then you use that as a shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, when were the trenches dug in Jezestica? You said it was later. When?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, after the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before 7th of January, 1993, then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the trenches were dug, there was some other structure used as a defence line; is that right? You mentioned a road which goes quite deep and you used that as a shelter. Isn't that what you were referring to as a defence line which existed before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road, like I said, we would take the road and bend down, because its sides are quite steep, and then when you come out to Brdo, it's quite high, and then you could see everything, if somebody wanted to look, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... different way. You told us you had a village guard to protect the houses. Weren't the village guards patrolling up on Brdo? That's where they were patrolling, because that was the line facing the Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others had that. I myself and three more, altogether four of us, we remained down there. We didn't go up there. There were others who were on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On duty, patrolling in Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us the attack on that day first came from Rankovici. Isn't it right that there was a recoilless cannon in Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing that from you now. I would have heard it when it went off, at least. No, there was none of that. This is a lie, a complete lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying there were no -- let's treat a broader area. You're saying there was no heavy artillery in your area, and by that I would include Siljkovici and Vresinje in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it being in Siljkovici, and there was none in Jezestica. But I don't know about it being in Siljkovici. But I know that there is nothing in Jezestica. Otherwise, you wouldn't have 45 people killed had they had something to defend themselves with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Siljkovici there was a possibility that there was Serb artillery positioned, positioned there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us the other day how you would call to each other from hamlet to hamlet, because it was very peaceful and tranquil there. Surely if a cannon was firing in Siljkovici, that's something you would have heard.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go over there from Jezestica. I told you, I had cattle, so until noon I was with Nikola and then in the afternoon I was with Mitar and Milenko. Once we finished the guards duty, I went to my own house. I would harvest the corn. I would cultivate the corn and so on. I'm telling you the truth. I didn't do anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Miladinovic. And if you see me making a gesture like this, it means I'd appreciate it if you would stop, because the interpretation runs on and we will be here a long time if it continues like this. What I would like to ask you in relation to 8th of August still, 1992, is the following: You told us the other day that when you first saw attackers, when you saw the attackers, you said that in that situation, you don't go up and shake hands with the attackers; you ran as fast as you can. That's what you told us. My question to you is this: Isn't that what you did on the 8th of August, 1992, when you saw attackers arriving, you ran for your life?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I tell you about that? I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you don't need to tell your whole story. My question is: Isn't it right, when you saw the attackers arriving, you ran as fast as you could to get away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what did I say when I ran off, if you're recording this correctly? Please don't skip over anything. Just read back what I said when I fled. Don't be taking me back and forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, if you like, I can read back to you what you said. You were asked if you recognised any of the -- Mr. Miladinovic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you should read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said: "Who were they? I didn't exactly go there to shake hands. How could I recognise them? How was I supposed to recognise them? It was impossible to recognise them. You don't do that sort of thing in Bosnia, go over there and shake hands. What you have to do is run as fast as you can." Now, that's what you said. My question is: Isn't that what you did; you ran as fast as you could when you saw the attackers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why didn't you read back what I said? There are lawyers, there are things there when I fled. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, look at me, please. Please answer the question that has been put to you. On the 8th of August, when you saw the attackers attacking, did you stay there or did you flee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said: Don't shoot, Chetniks. Catch the Turks alive. And I ran away. And I came back. None of my things were taken, not a single chicken, cow, or ox was taken away from me. Nothing. But I fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's important, Your Honour, I need to pursue it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You fled. As soon as you had said those words you ran away; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... look back until you got to Polje, down in the -- what you call Polje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you reached Polje, that's, what, 500 metres from Brdo? What's the distance between Polje and Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. It can be closer or farther away. But it was about 800 metres, perhaps, from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us on Friday that you saw what you call Turks burning houses and that they were in civilian clothes and olive-drab uniforms. Now, firstly, I want to ask you on that subject: You told us today that your people, people who were killed, were also wearing olive-drab uniforms. So that's right, isn't it? People in Jezestica, Serbs, were also wearing olive-drab uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were and some were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the olive-drab uniforms that you're referring to are the old uniforms of the JNA, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're aware, aren't you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tito's uniforms. Did we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware, aren't you, that Serbs, during the war wore the old JNA uniforms, not Muslims because a Muslim in an old JNA uniform was liable to get shot by his own side? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe he killed a Serb and took it from him or maybe he was given such a uniform. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it this way --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it this way to you, Mr. Miladinovic. Serbs in Jezestica wearing olive-drab uniforms, the attackers also wearing olive-drab uniforms, don't you see a danger there that people are going to end up killing people on the same side? I ask you that question because I put it to you that that can't be right, that the attackers weren't wearing olive-drab uniforms, as you've said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you for sure that that is correct. You have Naser there. They had their own personal signs. Please stop messing with me. I'm such an old person, and you're talking about some political things here. I come here to tell you what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, take it easy. It will soon be over. I'm here to protect you. The other two Judges are here with me to protect you, and we will protect you when there is a need to protect you. But for the time being, I think there is no need. You are taking good care of yourself. You are a very capable man. And please try to answer the questions that build Jones is putting to you. The moment he puts a question that we believe should not be put to you or that you shouldn't answer, we will intervene and we will tell you, Mr. Miladinovic, you don't need to answer this question. But so far, there haven't been any of these questions. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also right, isn't it, that there was nothing distinctive marking out the attackers, if we can call them that, for the sake of convenience, no distinctive markings, no insignia or anything of that kind, which you saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any badges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that actually most of the people were in civilian clothes on that day, most of the people you saw attacking the village, that they weren't in uniforms at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some did and -- some were and some weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, also that there were women among them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The women were taking things away. They were looting. Of course there were some. I've already said that before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that they were banging pots and pans and household objects to try and scare the Serbs away? Isn't that something you saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. I said it once, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Must have been a pretty pathetic sight the women who were reduced to banging --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone. Otherwise the interpreters can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I need to move the microphone closer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the children also among the attackers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were a bit older, not those that were still very young. 15, 16 years old, well, yes, they had to carry things too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people were so hungry, weren't they, on that day that, as you told us on Friday, despite the gunfire and the mortal danger they were eating right there in the village that very day, you saw them eating during the attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw women and children eating in your village on the 8th of August, 1992, eating the objects they were taking, and not waiting to take them away from the village; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, yes. They were taking things away and, sure enough, they were eating whatever they found. Why wouldn't they have been eating?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were desperately hungry, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. How on earth should I know? I didn't really watch them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to what you saw. But you've used the word "Turks." Just for the record, the word "Turk" is very insulting for Muslims, isn't it? It's not a kind term to use.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, didn't I say that already? Since World War II, we used to call them Turks. I remember that as a child. And then Tito came along and proclaimed them undeclared. So they were Muslims. I am from Bosnia. I am from Bosnia. I don't know what else to call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it imply that they should go back to Turkey and that they don't belong in Bosnia, using that term?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you got my meaning, what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wouldn't call a Muslim friend a Turk to his face, would you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why shouldn't I? I used to go and see them. I'd visit them in their homes. That was the sort of tragedy that happened. I never thought this would turn out this way. I never had the faintest idea that it would be World War II all over again. We used to visit each other. I gave Ibrahim Muratovic, a Muslim from my village, money so he could build a house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the attack. The fact is, isn't it, that you didn't see any houses being set fire to on the 8th of August because, as you've told us, as soon as you saw the attackers and shouted, you fled as fast as you could, so you didn't actually see anything set on fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid. Why are you mucking me about like this? I was clear enough. I was running and houses were being set ablaze. Same thing all over again. We can't go on like this for 16 days, can we? Of course I did see. It was 20 metres away from me. He was exercising command. My house and Nikola's house, 30 metres from where I was standing. And again you're taking me back to that. I must have said this over 15 times now. Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, I know you're very keen to say that you saw houses burning, but what we have to establish is what you saw. You told us that you fled as soon as you shouted at the attackers. You told us you didn't turn back to look. You told us you went to Polje, which is 800 metres away I think you said. So isn't it correct that in fact you did not see houses being set fire to. You returned later and assumed that's that what had happened but you didn't see it with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My God. God forbid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me intervene myself here, because we are back to the same position we were when we were talking of the 7th of January. I'll just ask him one maximum two questions. On the 8th of August, on the 8th of August, there was this attack, and you fled. And you know, because you told us, that the number of houses were set on fire on that day. I know, because you have already said it, that you saw them burning, you saw these houses burning. Did you actually see with your own eyes anyone burning any of these houses, either while you were fleeing or after that you had already reached Polje? Did you see any one of these houses being set on fire? Not burning, but being set on fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, on the 8th of August, as I said, there may be as many as three or four statements back in Bosnia, and we have some here. It was an all-out attack against those villages and I was there when it burnt, when the villages were burning. 30 metres from where I was standing, the fire reached me and then I realised it was time to run, so I ran into the field. Two or three hours I was back. Everything was ablaze. I found dead bodies there. Do you want me to go through the whole story again giving you their first and last names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Miladinovic. I only want you to tell me whether you saw -- not that you saw these houses on fire. That you have already told us. What I want from you is only one answer: Did you see any of these houses being set on fire, or did you just see them burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want me to read out the names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whose houses were burning? Of course I saw it. Of course I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you see them burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did see them burning. Three hours later, I came back, and everything was burning, my house and my relatives' houses, I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you see any of those houses at the time when they were set on fire or were being set on fire, or were you escaping at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very outset, I saw them burned down all the way again. Am I not being clear enough? Three hours later when I was back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not being -- I am afraid you are not being clear. We are not interested, because you have already told us, in what you saw three hours later. What we are interested to know is whether you were there seeing any one of these particular houses at the very same moment when it was being set on fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fire. 50 of those houses I wasn't there when perhaps between 20 and 30 were being set alight. Did I run? Of course I ran. 30 houses burnt down. I saw it with my own eyes. Please don't try to confuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't helped us much, Mr. Miladinovic. We have started back where we started with no answer from you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'll proceed from that point of having no answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Mr. Miladinovic, that the Serbs counter-attacked that day, the 8th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. You said that wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'd refer you to a statement you gave in the year 2000 to ICTY investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the record, it's ERN 00940535, page 3, third sentence: "By that time, the reinforcements came from the Territorial Defence and we followed them and saw the Muslims withdrawing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember making that statement to ICTY investigators that the Serb Territorial Defence arrived and forced the Muslims to withdraw? You're going to have to speak louder for the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown a copy of his statement. Do Your Honours have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have the version in English, and we also have the version in B/C/S. I don't think it's going to serve you any purpose to show it to him. I would just tell him that you are going to read a part from his statement, and then if he wants to see it, we will show it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then ask him whether it's true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring, Mr. Miladinovic, to a statement which in the English has been signed by you as being truthful, and you said -- I put it to you that you said: "I saw that some of them were in old reserve service uniforms and some of them in civils. At that time the reinforcements came from the Territorial Defence and we followed them and saw the Muslims withdrawing. However, by this time all the houses in the downhill area of the village were set on fire," and it goes on. Isn't that right, that the Territorial Defence arrived that very day, 8th of August, 1992, and that's something which you told investigators when you were interviewed about this? Let me put it a different way, if you're having trouble answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Let me answer the question. I think it's clear enough, Mr. Jones. Do you remember saying this to the investigators of the Prosecutor, of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Miladinovic, namely, that after the attack, the Territorial Defence, the Serbian Territorial Defence, arrived and that you, together with others, followed them, and you saw the Muslims withdrawing? Do you remember saying this to the Prosecution or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. On the 8th of August, we were down in the field. Someone came, some army or other, and went up. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you do remember mentioning this to the Prosecution; no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Mr. Jones, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And didn't the army which came counter-attack with grenades and incendiary devices which also caused damage to the houses on Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single shell was fired. They had some weapons and they came up and there was a withdrawal. Then they strew flour and beans along the road to Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were fleeing, fleeing for their lives, and dropping the food which they had taken from your village when the Serb army counter-attacked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that not all houses, the houses in Brdo, were destroyed on the 8th of August. Firstly, some were damaged beforehand; for example, the house of your son Djordjo Miladinovic was not damaged in August, but in July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was set alight and razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th. June, not July. June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also the houses of Radojka Milanovic and Vlado Milanovic were not destroyed in August but in June?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radomir and this man, Vlado Jovanovic. Their houses remained. I wasn't lying. Those two were intact. They were not destroyed on the 8th of August. They came later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it also right: You told us that - and this is going ahead to the later attack, in January - that you thought of burning your own house --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll go slowly. On the 7th of January, you thought of burning your own house as you were leaving, but in fact you didn't do it. It's just something you considered, in it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perish the thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you told us today, was it not, that you thought: Maybe I should burn my house before I run. And I ask you that question --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You didn't understand me. It was the other man in Kajici where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how we understood him. It wasn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was with Mitar Nikolic, Mitar was the one who wanted to do that. I would never have wanted to burn my own house, because I was the one who built it up. I may not be an educated man, but it seems that I have a better understanding of things than you do. Please don't ask me this sort of question. You're twisting things about. This is an international court of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Enough, Mr. Miladinovic. Mr. Jones, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, my apologies if I suggested that you considered it. But isn't it right that Serbs would sometimes burn their own houses or barns rather than allow it to be captured by the enemy, when they had to withdraw? Not you, but other Serbs would do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single citizen of Jezestica would ever do that. I swear upon my life that I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, question about livestock which went missing after the 8th of August, 1992. Are you able to tell us how much livestock was actually stolen as opposed to livestock which got loose during the attack and just wandered off? Is that something you can help us with or are you not able to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say precisely which cows were stolen and which cows --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which chickens ran away as opposed to being stolen by someone? You can help us with that? Isn't it correct, Mr. Miladinovic, that anyone --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that anyone, old men, women, or children, could have taken livestock, and equally, foxes or wild animals could have destroyed the livestock? You're not able to say cow by cow, pig by pig, chicken by chicken, what happened to each one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all burnt down immediately, and everything was being taken. And chickens and oxen and hens taken away. Nothing there. Do you understand me? The cow goes and the ox goes and the goats go, and everything that was there just goes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know, do you, who took any of those livestock?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who was setting fire to things and who was killing the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on. Didn't you also say, and wouldn't you agree, that actually, I think these were your words, that it would be a shame to leave livestock there while the village is burning because they could actually get killed during the course of the burning, so it's better to evacuate them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had driven the cattle away. It was -- the cattle was better off that way than being burned alive. Well, you had to make some use of it. I think that was a good idea. Those were the times. It was wartime, after all. That's how it was, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after the attack of the 8th of August, 1992, you said that you received rubber boots and shirts. Now, who provided you with rubber boots and shirts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how did you come upon them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How am I supposed to say who from, who brought it? It may have been someone else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't simply return home and find rubber boots and shirts in your wardrobe, did you? I mean, these were issued, were they not, by the army, the VRS, as part of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean, "issued."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided with uniforms after the 8th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the 7th of January, 1993. Now, isn't it right that it was dark when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot follow the proceedings because the witness is constantly interrupting the speakers. The interpreters cannot follow the proceedings because the witness is constantly interrupting the speakers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're done with the 8th of August. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, may I please remind you, and please obey me for my sake, that you answer the questions that are put to you. And if you want to say something else, put up your finger, draw my attention, and I will decide after consulting with the other two Judges whether to give you permission to go ahead or not. But while others are speaking, please refrain from speaking yourself. Because here we have a system of interpretation. People have to -- behind those glasses have to listen to what Mr. Jones is saying, to what I am saying, to what you are saying, and then everything has to be translated, either into Serbo-Croat or into English or into French. Yes. Tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief. When we set out -- when we started with the 8th of August, I think we should finish with that. The people who were killed, I can tell him about all this misery and then the whole world and you who are here, and he's mucking me about. And about Christmas, the things that I forgot to say. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, please try to understand that if we were to allow every single witness in this Tribunal to come over and tell us the entire story according to him or to her, we would never finish. The system doesn't work like that. You answer the questions that are put to you. When Mr. Jones is finished, if there is anything else you would like to add, tell me what you would like to add and we will see what we can grant you to say. But for the time being, you need -- for the time being, and please don't interrupt me, for the time being, you need to answer the questions that Mr. Jones is putting to you. So, Mr. Jones, now move to the 7th of January, please, and let's try and finish as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed, Your Honour. All the questions I'll put will require only a yes or a no answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed. Hope springs eternal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, it was dark, wasn't it, on the 7th of January, 1993, when the attack started? It was 5.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it was. But I didn't finish what I was saying before. I'm just not happy with this, with not being allowed to finish. I don't think this is being done properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but let us decide. We are the Judges here, Mr. Miladinovic, and as I explained to you, there are rules that have to be followed here. Yes, Mr. Jones. Next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw -- when you saw flames on that morning, you didn't know how houses had been set on fire, if they had been set on fire by people or during the attack, do you; you simply saw flames?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, that's not fair, Mr. Jones, because he was asked about the torching of houses before on the 7th of January and he was very categoric that there were some -- few houses that he saw being set on fire with his own eyes. So the way you've put it, you're asking him to go back on what he has already testified under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Well, Your Honour, I meant to refer to houses which were burning before the ones which he says he saw. But it doesn't matter. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you saw thousands and thousands of people attacking the village that day? Isn't it right that these were thousands of men, women, children, people in civilian clothes, an absolute mixed bag of people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that. You want me to go through that again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 7th -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish. You have agreed that that was the case, that this huge number of persons was a mixed crowd. Next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was absolute chaos, wasn't it, that morning, a chaotic scene?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said how you saw people in all sorts of clothes. You said black and white clothes, "like we had." Now, you've told us that you didn't have uniforms, so when you say "black and white clothes like we had," you mean civilian clothes again, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just not happy with the way this is being conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Black and white clothes like civilians, I don't know what my learned friend mean with it, but he doesn't make it clear whenever he was referring then to the clothes compared with the villagers of Jezestica or the clothes the attackers were wearing, while meanwhile he had put straightforward in his answering on his examination and using the label of it, which I will not repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't see that that clarifies matters but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't in the least. Mr. Miladinovic, please look at me. You mentioned earlier and you've just been reminded that in the course of your testimony you said that the attackers were wearing white and black clothes "like we were." These white and black clothes, were they white and black uniforms or white and black civilian clothes? What did you mean when you said "white and black clothes, like we had"? Civilian clothes or uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] White, like snow, camouflage, to attract more easily, or black, glass, if you know what a glass is, camouflage. Everyone was camouflaging. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "like we had," you've also told us that you weren't given uniforms. So did you have uniforms or were they -- these people wearing what you were wearing; namely, civilian clothes? Which is it? It can't be both.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. You need to repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Amongst the Serbian population that was defending the town of Jezestica, were there any wearing white camouflage uniforms, among the Serbian, your colleagues, in other words. Were there any wearing white uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were there any wearing black camouflage uniforms amongst the Serb --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Not that either. No. I'm speaking about the Serbs now. They were wearing different clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now let's talk about the attackers. Were there any attackers that you noticed who were wearing white camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did see that. I told you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Black clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: White or black, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both white and black. On one side, they were people in white clothing, and then on the other, in black, and so on. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are right, because you already told us this before, but when you mentioned it before, you said that they were wearing white and black, "like we were," meaning like the Serbs were. Were the Serbs wearing the same kind of clothes or not? Because if they weren't, you need to explain to us why before you said they were wearing white and black, "like we were."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. I don't remember that I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you did. I can assure you that you did. And Mr. Jones is perfectly right in questioning you on this, because it calls for an explanation. Because if, as you've just stated, the Serbs defending the town of Jezestica were not wearing any white uniforms or were not wearing any black uniforms, why did you before say that the Muslims were -- or the attackers were wearing white and black uniforms, "like we were," if you weren't wearing white and black uniforms, why did you say "like we were"? Or was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it a mistake of the tongue, a lapse -- Yes, Mr. Jones, I think you can proceed to something different.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, again on that day, you were afraid and running for your life, were you not; you were fleeing the scene as soon as you could?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're talking of the 7th of January now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would you like me to tell you? Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that on that day, seeing another attack, that you were again concerned with fleeing and not sticking around?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed there for a while. There were eight of us there, and when we saw that from Jaglici, the whole field was full of soldiers, and from Simici and Magasici, there was a group coming to the attack. And then on the other side, from Jaglici, there was a bunch of people there: This was the attack at 5.30. So I was on guard. I happened to be on guard, and I was observing that. And I said: Brothers, let's hope that we stay alive. This is not turning out to be a good Christmas for us. I didn't even eat anything. I didn't eat any pecanica [phoen]. I left it all behind, the cured meat, the rakija. I left it all to the Turks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you told us, nonetheless, that you saw 10 to 15 houses being set on fire that day. You told us again that these were by, I think six people, you said, in olive-grey uniforms. Now, my first question is: Where were you when you saw these houses burning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Again you are taking me back to the 8th of August. This happened on the 8th of August. I said that before. And you're taking me constantly back to there. I've already said that 20 times. Let's go to the 7th of January. You're constantly taking me back to the 8th of August. Please. I told you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, please stop. He is not taking you back to the 8th of August. The question that he put to you refers to the 7th of January. And please try to answer. You said earlier on that you saw on the 7th of January some houses being set on fire. While they were being set on fire. Mr. Jones would like to know the exact position of yourself, where you were, at the time when you claim to have seen these houses being set on fire. Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. On the 7th of January, I was in front of my house when, like I said, they were coming in camouflage uniforms and in black. I saw on one side four people; then on the other side I saw six men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer, then, is you were at your house. Now, what I want to ask you is: When you were standing outside your house and all these attackers came, some or many of whom had weapons, surely you weren't just standing in front of your house 10 or 15 metres away watching all this happen, because you would have got shot or you would have been liable to get shot. So my question to you is: Were you really outside your house watching all this happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true I was. But I fled up to Brdo. From those three houses when you go up to Brdo, above Tanici, then you can see the whole of Kravica spreading before you. And only about 20 houses is it not possible to see. And then you can read that I watched them as they were burning it. This is a woods. It's a sort of sheltered spot in Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, you told us on Friday that you could barely see -- you couldn't see a kilometre away. I think you said that it was hard for you to see even 20 metres away. I'm not entirely sure what your evidence was now. But you've told us today that Brdo is 800 metres from Polje. So you're not saying, are you, that from Brdo, 800 metres away, you could see people going into houses and setting fire to them and all the things you've described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe he wouldn't be able to identify them, but not to see individuals at 800 metres, come on, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think it's possible to see colours at 800 metres, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course you can see colours at 800 metres, especially if you have green as contrast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's turn to these people who you saw and you've told us that you saw on the 7th of January, again, people in olive-drab uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it right that on the 8th of August, there were people in olive-drab uniforms setting fire to houses and also on the 7th of January, 1993, people in olive-drab uniforms, and they were the only ones who were actually setting fire to houses? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th, that is correct. As for the 7th of January, that is a different team. There were more soldiers there who -- there were many soldiers. Everything was surrounded. Kravica and all of the other Serb villages. And at a certain point in time, all -- there was shooting erupting from all over the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We need to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes. How much more do you have with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Probably half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you have a re-examination, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If so, limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You need to think whether to keep the other witness here or whether -- because if it's half an hour plus -- basically three-quarters of an hour that we have left, plus there is another matter that I would like to bring to your attention and which I will need to address at the end of today's hearing. So please decide whether to retain the witness, the next witness here, or whether to send him to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you want to learn this now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's up to you. I mean, I'm just telling you this so that you know how to make your own arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's 25-minutes break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think Mr. Wubben wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Very short. Thank you. Very short, Your Honour. We sent the projected witness subsequently planned, we sent him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Yes. One moment, Mr. Jones, because age takes precedence here. Yes, Mr. Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot one person. At Christmas, I forgot Milovan Ostojic. Please. And then I have the place where my sister was married, my cousin. That's where I got married, the village of Zagornik [phoen]. I can give you more details if you wish. I can tell you immediately. That's where one child was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do not require that information. We know all about it already. Mr. Jones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, before the break, we left off with you in Brdo, above the village of Jezestica, on the 7th of January, 1993. Looking down at the thousands of people who were swarming into the Polje part of Jezestica. And now so I want to ask you your impression from the hill, looking down at all of this. Isn't it right that what you saw was effectively a swarm of people, thousands of people, all among the houses, mixed up among themselves, in other words, a scene of complete pandemonium?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. When it comes to thousands of people, I have put forward to this witness a clarifying question that he saw indeed many people, but when it comes to the attack of Jezestica, he limited that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was a thousand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he limited that number. He repeated that it was thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My learned friend confirmed that it was a thousand. Yes, indeed. That's what I recall. Not thousands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, this is a thousand people, is it not, in a very small area of your village that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it right that these people, women, children, civilians, were all mixed up among each other, among the houses, and it would be very difficult for you to actually see what any one of them was doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke earlier about groups of people, as if there were one group doing one thing and another group doing another thing. But isn't it right that in fact what you saw is certain activities - looting, burning, attacking - that it was all happening at the same time, in the same area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So isn't it also right that from your spot on the hill, 800 metres away, you weren't noticing this person has entered this house with a flask or container, and this other person has come out of this other house carrying this item. You weren't actually able to see that precisely, what was happening in each case, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw them on the 8th of August, but on the 7th, for Christmas, it was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Couldn't it be that what you saw on the 7th of January, 1993 was fighters going through your village and then women and children and civilians behind them doing whatever they had to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you repeat your answer, please, Witness. You said trebelor [phoen] or something.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what? Because I asked to speak or do you want me to repeat something else? I'm not sure exactly what it is you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it also right that for days after the attack on the 7th of January, 1993, that there were marauding bands of scavenging people taking whatever they could from houses, food, and indeed roof tiles and anything which they needed to survive that winter? If you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was being done by the Turks in my village. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... days after the attack of the 7th of January, 1993, not just on the day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's not quite clear. I did not perhaps clarify that. Perhaps I need to give a better explanation of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I'll come back to that. Let me ask you first about your cow which you said was recovered. You got your cow back, I think, after the 7th of January. Can you tell us first of all when that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was when? That was when Srebrenica fell. A man brought it to Bratunac. I can recognise my cow. He found it in Pale. It's my own cow. I've had it -- I'd had it for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a Serb who gave you back your cow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't give it back to me. I begged him to do so, but he didn't return it to me. And my oxen had been taken to Cizmici, and I can tell you who did that by name if you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simply this: The person who wouldn't give your cow back to you was a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's a Serb. What is true is true. I am an old man and I don't need to lie. So don't you either burden me in different ways. I need to know that exactly. Because I didn't go to any schools. I'm a self-taught man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us when you returned to your village after the 7th of January, 1993, on what date you first went back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the exact date, but I returned after 70 days to gather the dead. I stated that and I could see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us how you went back to the village and you gathered the bodies. Isn't it right that in those 70 days, wild animals could have caused a lot if not all of the damage to the corpses which you found?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I did not see how it happened, but this is how it was: My son was buried. His head was cut off and then it was removed, as well as the legs and the arms. But the body was buried. And the others I found out in the open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you're familiar with this area, aren't you? It's right, isn't it, that there are wild animals in the woods and forests which would be very likely to interfere with corpses which are left out in the open and which could have caused them to be scattered in the way that you found them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that there are animals. I'm not going to lie about it. It's true that there are animals around, but I didn't see how this came about. But there were no bodies, there were no heads. There's no animal that could eat a head. It's hard. But there were no heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it also right that that was the first opportunity you had, 70 days later, to see the damage which had been done to the houses in Jezestica, and Polje in particular?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw everything when I came back. I went around everywhere. We had a mill. That was also set on fire. And that's a shame. It's a waste. Because you could use it to bake bread. There was also the local community hall. That was all smashed up. I didn't write down that these people were killed by Turks. That's what the sign said. It said that these were victims of the fascists from World War II. I don't see why this had to be destroyed and smashed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But isn't it right that in the 70 days in between you leaving your village and coming back, a great deal of the damage which you saw could have occurred or could have been done by people who in the meantime passed through the area and could have been done indeed by a Serb counter-attack to capture, recapture that area? It's possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something about that? No, no. I must say something. Nobody went there, in that area, during those 70 days. No Serb went there. Not one Serb went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you weren't there during the 70 days, so you didn't see anything of what happened in that time, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee that 100 per cent. I guarantee 100 per cent that no one went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that when you went back to the village that nothing was left standing. But you also told us that some houses only suffered 20 per cent damage, whereas others were more damaged. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's correct. That's what I said. Those in Polje were more solidly built, as opposed to the ones in Brdo which were not so solid. Even the chickens were burned. I had a well, so I put in two canisters of jam into this well. If you know what this looks like, it only has a kind of wooden roof over it. And even that was burned. Nothing was left. All the buildings that were made out of lighter material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask if the witness could be shown one of the photographic exhibits 01087870. I can provide my copy. I don't know if otherwise it could be put on the monitor. In fact, I wonder if it could be placed on the ELMO. That might be best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that we can all see it, Mr. Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recognise this, but you're free to look at it. But really, I cannot recognise it. There's no need to do that. I don't need it. I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at that house - even if you don't recognise it - isn't it right that that's actually been damaged by mortar, mortar fire, rather than by fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What makes you think that the witness is in a position or is capable of answering that question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He survived the war, Your Honour, and he's no doubt seen mortar damage. If the witness can help with that. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you can't -- Mr. Miladinovic, can you answer that question? Would you be able by looking at this photo to tell us how that house came to be damaged that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to tell you? A shell hit it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A shell hit it. Precisely. Thank you. I'm going to move on to another area altogether, so we can remove the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the same time, I noticed that there was something written down this photograph, and I don't know what it was, but when it is block letters, the witness stated on Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It has been folded. The paper has been folded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly my copy was folded and he's being shown nothing more than the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It was folded, because I was keeping a watchful eye because I knew there was writing there and I also heard Mr. Jones to tell the usher to fold it, to hide the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And since the witness is illiterate, it shouldn't matter too much in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And again my learned friend - and that's towards the Judges - he stated that on Friday that he could read block letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed and not waste time on these petty issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, I'm going to ask you some final questions now about the start of the war, so I'm actually going back in time. First of all, if you can help us with this: Isn't it right that people from Serbia came to Jezestica to help you fight against what you would call the Turks, volunteers from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know Andjelko Mladjenovic, don't you? Or you knew him.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andjelko Mladjenovic. Of course I know him. I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... came from Serbia to fight in your area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born there. He had a brother named Dragan, who was killed, and his mother was killed too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mihajlo Uzelac? Is that name familiar to you? Mihajlo Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First time I hear of the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the war started with Serbs being expelled from Bukova Glava in May 1992. But isn't it right that Serbs had been killing and expelling Muslims from the Podrinje area from mid-April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where from? Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... from the Drina River, from the Drina Valley. From your area, Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly know what you're driving at. I'm not sure what I should answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's deal with something closer to your village. In Hranca, are you aware that on the 2nd of May 1992, so before the 5th of May, 1992, Serbs killed four Muslims, burnt 43 houses, and later killed 19 more Muslims from Hranca in the Vuk Karadzic school? Is that something you might have heard about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. Quite frankly, I work as a farmer. I never budged from my village until the 7th of January. I said it about a hundred times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we know about --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife left for Serbia. That's sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miladinovic. We know that you know about Bijeceva because you mentioned it on Friday. So let's turn to Bijeceva which I think you'll confirm was a Muslim village before the war, Bijeceva, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bijeceva. I said a while ago that Bijeceva, didn't I, or should I say it. Do you know what a mill is, a flour mill?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, could you please just answer my question. Isn't it right that Bijeceva was a Muslim village before the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of it. Not all of it. There were also homes in Bukova Glava, the village of Bijeceva. What I'm telling you is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were Muslims living in Bijeceva in May 1992, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if the usher could put a map on the ELMO, and it's really for our benefit as much as for the witness just so we can see these places. I've highlighted --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's pointless for me to look at this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Miladinovic. It's for us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's pointless. And the image is a slant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it, Mr. Miladinovic. This is not for you; it's for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you zoom out a bit more. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I've highlighted Jezestica, Glogova, Bijeceva, Bukova Glava and Zagoni?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, do you know Radoje Gvozdenovic from Magasici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radivoje Gvozdenovic? That's not where he's from. He's from Zagoni. You know you're make a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zagoni. Thank you. For that correction.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a relative of mine. The son of my sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- thank you. Do you know Milisav Deronjica from Zagoni. Milisav Deronjica from Zagoni?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know - just two more names - Petar Dimitrijevic from Zagoni?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, do you know Petar Ilic from Zagoni?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard him say "I don't know." The question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you know Petar Ilic from Zagoni?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you knew the first three names I mentioned. Did you know that they were all in Bijeceva around the same time that you were, namely, on the 5th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't with them, but I know all of them, because I told you that my sister lived there, married to someone from the village. You have it exactly how many men were killed there and how many children were taken away. This is something that should be written down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that you in the hamlet of Bukova Glava, village of Bijeceva on the 5th of May 1992 not just to celebrate a friend's naming day on the next day but to disarm Muslims in Bijeceva?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see how someone is twisting things around. It's a disgrace. It's a sin. Because that village --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask you to refer to the Exhibit D89, which has already been entered in evidence, a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, isn't the witness allowed to answer the question? Because he was starting to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness was given a very inflammatory answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He obviously said -- he obviously did not agree with the question or what was being suggested to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I'm going to suggest to you now, Mr. Miladinovic, and I'm referring to Exhibit D89, page 5, where there's reference to the crime in Bijeceva on the 6th of May, 1992 -- I'll read from that. "6th of May, 1992, village of Bijeceva was attacked from the direction of Zagoni and Bratunac. Nine Bosniak houses were torched and an old man Ibro Jasarevic was killed. The SDS leaders who attacked the village were Radoj Gvozdenovic from Zagoni, Milisav Deronjica from Zagoni, Petar Dmitrovic, Petar Ilic from Zagoni and others."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pausing there, did you hear that Ibro Jasarevic was killed on the 6th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Muslim after all, so why should you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just didn't hear, because I didn't go there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, please refrain from passing comments like you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying you're not aware this happened in Bijeceva, this torching of Bosniak houses, on the 6th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you that when you described today men in olive-drab JNA uniforms setting fire to houses in Jezestica, you're confused and what you're in fact remembering is what Serbs did in Bijeceva and not what you saw in Jezestica? Now thinking about it, is that something you would agree with? You've confused Serbs in JNA uniforms setting fire to houses with what you say you saw in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just answer yes or no, Mr. Miladinovic, please. Mr. Miladinovic, just answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is erroneous information. This is false. This is not true, the way you're putting it. Why are you trying to confuse me? I've Told you everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wubben, do you have any questions on re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Only one limited --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Only one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You switched it off now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Only one limited issue, Your Honour. It's related to the cow that had been taken away from the witness. Re-examined by Mr. Wubben:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have one question for you. When you tried to get your cow back from that Serb, that happened a few -- a few years later than attack, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think you should clarify. Then I can tell you exactly. Can you please make this a bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you meant that was during the time that Srebrenica fall, did you mention the year 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The cow was brought to Bratunac. My wife recognised it and I recognised it. We'd had it for 15 years. It had been in Pale. I asked the man to give it back to me, but he refused. I do not wish to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you find out that it was a Serb who took away the cow or did the Serb get it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A Muslim or Turk took it away, as you like, or undeclared, or Bosniak, whatever you choose to call them. Srebrenica fell, so it remained, and another man brought it back to Bratunac for himself, not to bring the cow back to me. I think you keep misunderstanding me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Eser. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just with regard to the cow. You told us that the cow was taken away from Muslims, but did you ask --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes. But then the cow was held by a Serb. And did you have any information how the cow which, according to your memory or according to your assumption, was stolen by Muslims came to a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left -- the Muslims left their homes, so he went and he found it there at Pale. That's how. I couldn't start a fight with that man. The cow was gone, so it was gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Another question. When you have been asked whether you know Andjelko Mladjenovic. You told us that you know him. Now, did you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mladjenovic. Not Miladinovic. Mladjenovic. That was the last name. We must get this right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, last question. You made statements in the year 2000, and all statements, all pages are signed by you. Now, before you put your signature there, had you read what was written on the page or did you just sign the page without having read it before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Signature is on the English version, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The signature is always on the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So it was only that he had seen it, yeah. Thank you. So I don't have another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Dragomir Miladinovic, look at me. Finally it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finally it's over. We are finished with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
