utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can't be over. It's never over. You know how many of my relatives were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are many others who are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask you to -- just two minutes to read the names out. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Read the names out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, the village of Zagoni, 12th of July, my sister's son, Mile, was killed. My grandson, Miko. Mother-in-law Mileva, Radoj Gvozdenovic was also killed, Drago was killed. Rada, my granddaughter, was killed too. Miodrag Milosevic and Dragisa, two brothers. Ljubica and Sana's wife, whose name I can't remember. She was killed. These three persons and their child was taken away to Pale. Then Milos Milosevic, Vidosav Gvozdenovic Blagoje. Thank you very much, Your Honours. This is all I have. Thank you so much for giving me a chance to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Miladinovic. Your testimony finishes here. There are many --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are thousands -- there are thousands in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia who have suffered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put this back in my pocket. And these you can throw away. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, will you please listen to what I have to tell you. Mr. Miladinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are thousands who, like you, in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia, have suffered as much, and perhaps even more, than you have, and they come from all ethnicities. Some of them are Serbs, some of them are, according to you, Turks, Bosniaks, Muslims, call them whatever you like, some of them are Croats, some of them are of different nationalities. You're not the only one who has suffered in that war. There are many, many other thousands that have suffered in that war. And this Tribunal opens its doors to all ethnicities to come here and tell us the truth, all ethnicities. And we allow you to mention names and give details because we consider that this is important for the process of reconciliation that this Tribunal also has the duty to try and promote. It's probable that when you wake up in the morning and before you go to bed at night, you think about the tragedy that occurred in your country and possibly convince yourself that only Serbs were killed during that war. Not only Serbs were killed; many Muslims were killed, many Croats were killed, many others were killed. So before I ask Madam Usher to escort you out of this courtroom, my last few words to you is: When I hear you say -- refer to the Muslims as "Turks," I don't think you really believe in promoting reconciliation. You are still stuck to the past. You're living stuck to the past. I know it's not easy to disengage from the past, but you're living -- you are a slave of the past. People like you who have had these bad experiences, World War II and now the war in 19 -- in the 1990s, they should be in the forefront to teach your children and your grandchildren that war doesn't pay. It causes sorrow and tear and loss. So I'm sending you back home, hoping that a man of your experience will preach love and brotherhood and reconciliation to your folk. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this trial. Madam Usher will escort you out of this courtroom. You will receive all the assistance that you need to facilitate your return back home. And on behalf of everyone present, I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I thank this court for hearing me out. I told you everything I know. I thank you so much. I don't regret coming here. It was a very pleasant experience. Thanks to all the personnel also for understanding me. God bless you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Give them back to him. Give them back to him. If he doesn't want them, throw them away. There is a very quick thing, matter, that I would like to raise with you. I wish to draw your attention, Madam Vidovic and Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that one of the results of the discussions held at the plenary last week was to amend, inter alia, Rule 98 bis. The amendments which have already been made public will come into force on the 17th of December. I'm informing you about this, or reminding you, or I mean drawing your attention about this, because obviously both of you will have to rethink a little bit the schedule to be applied as soon as the case for the Prosecution comes to a close. Because there is obviously not going to be any significant time span during which you will spend efforts and Prosecution will spend efforts and we'll spend efforts on trying to reach a decision in terms of the new Rule 98 bis. The whole procedure will be as speedy as we think will be necessary, given the circumstances, because obviously we don't know now what the position is going to be at the end of the case for the Prosecution. But please be informed that it will be a quite -- a speedy procedure that will be applied and everything will be submitted orally and not in writing. And that includes also our decision. But in particular, it's very important for you because it certainly would require you to rethink the time that you need to finish your investigations and also the time when you will be bringing forward witnesses should the Trial Chamber decide that it's not a case of acquittal, in whole or in part. So you need to prepare your witnesses that may be what you thought may be happening in I don't know which month, maybe anticipated by one or two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It might be useful at some stage for us to have an indication, and I need to consult the new Rule 98 bis, but of how long it would be envisaged that we would be allowed to prepare our witnesses, prepare purely the Defence part of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That you will have the usual -- I mean, I can guarantee you -- I mean, obviously we haven't discussed dates, Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, but don't expect us to be unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Still something like a two-month period, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: What did you mention? Two months?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To prepare the case for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: An indication at some stage would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It also depends on what we will decide under the Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, yes. It was simply because I was aware of this rule change was coming. I wasn't sure whether it meant we would still have the same period of time but that we would simply be preparing our defence case at that stage or whether that whole period would be reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will depend, Mr. Jones. That will depend. But our idea was to just put you on the alert that the procedure has changed and it will be applied as changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And basically it would also mean that if, according to -- but I might as well skip that, because it's certainly not going to be the case. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. I think it's in this same courtroom.
